passage: Sunday night. A third person asked me to mentor them this week, and I said no. It was awkward. Last spring I had four mentees plus the release crunch, and I cancelled on two of them; one went quiet and I'm not sure I ever fixed that. So the rule now: two at a time, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, forty-five minutes, and I say so upfront. Hemant is one of my two, and I'd rather give Hemant a reliable slot than a maybe. Wrote to the third person offering to recommend a colleague and a date when I might have space. Felt guilty for an hour, then fine. Sessions kept beat sessions promised. — Tejas

passage:
In Nanded, word had spread that Nandini, who worked at the bank and had cleared a tough engineering entrance herself, mentored students on Sundays. By June, six parents had asked. Disha, whose daughter was in Class 11, came to the house with a box of pedas and a hopeful face.
Nandini made tea and thought it through before answering. Last year she had said yes to five students and ended up cancelling half the Sundays and rushing the rest. 'Two is what I can do well,' she said. 'I have two now, until December.' She wrote her Sunday hours on a slip of paper: 10 to 12, only those. 'I can take your daughter from January. Until then, she can come to the free doubt session I hold on the first Sunday of each month.'
Disha nodded slowly and left the pedas anyway.

qa.q: What might Disha have been feeling when she arrived?
qa.a: Disha was hopeful and a little anxious, wanting help for her daughter in Class 11.

qa.q: Why is it wise for Nandini to take only two students?
qa.a: Last year five students meant cancelled Sundays and rushed help; two lets her give each student reliable time.

qa.q: How might Disha's daughter be affected by the answer?
qa.a: She has to wait until January, but gets a reliable place then and the monthly doubt session meanwhile.

grounding: It shows a mentor who has learnt that overcommitting leads to missed sessions, taking only two students at a time and stating availability clearly.
